terms.grammar: pronoun: genitive of is; it does not change with the thing owned
evidence: Cic. Sen. 31: ex ejus linguā melle dulcior fluēbat ōrātiō
terms.comment: Use ejus when “his” is not the subject of the clause: Crates struck paedagōgum ejus, the boy’s tutor. When “his” is the subject’s own, Latin uses suus: “Esau ran to meet frātrī suō (his own brother) … and clasped collum ejus (his, the brother’s, neck)”.

terms.grammar: pronoun (possessive, reflexive), first and second declension
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.59: invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs
terms.comment: Refers back to the subject of its clause, or in reported speech and purpose clauses to the subject of the main verb. It agrees with the thing owned: ad suōs, to his own men.

phrases.latin: Currēns itaque Esau obviam frātrī suō, amplexātus est eum: stringēnsque collum ejus, et ōsculāns flēvit.
phrases.english: So Esau ran to meet his brother and embraced him, and clasping his neck and kissing him, he wept.

phrases.latin: ut Cratēs, cum indoctum puerum vīdisset, paedagōgum ejus percussit
phrases.english: as Crates, when he saw an ignorant boy, struck the boy’s tutor

phrases.latin: ex ejus linguā melle dulcior fluēbat ōrātiō
phrases.english: from his tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey

phrases.latin: ita sīc armātus in Tiberim dēsiluit multīsque superincidentibus tēlīs incolumis ad suōs trānāvit
phrases.english: So, armed as he was, he leapt into the Tiber, and under a hail of missiles swam across unhurt to his own men.

phrases.latin: invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs, venit ipse mātūrē, scalmum nūllum videt.
phrases.english: The next day Canius invites his friends; he comes early himself and sees not a single boat.
